## Tidy

Refers to *tidy data*

::: {style="font-size:75%;"}
> "Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way."\
> --- Leo Tolstoy

> "Tidy datasets are all alike, but every messy dataset is messy in its own way."\
> --- Hadley Wickham
:::

Tidy data follow a consistent set of organizational principles

Typically a bit more work up front but **much** easier to work with after

## Tidy: Principles

Three rules to a tidy dataset

1. Each variable is a column; each column is a variable.

2. Each observation is a row; each row is an observation.

3. Each value is a cell; each cell is a single value.

![](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/images/tidy-1.png)

::: footer
<https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-tidy.html#fig-tidy-structure>
:::


## Tidy: Why Tidy?

1. Consistency! Any sort of consistency in your data management will be beneficial.

::: fragment
2. R loves vectors! Having variables in columns plays well with many functions.
:::

::: fragment
3. Cohesion with an ecosystem of R packages that expect tidy data.
:::


## Long vs. Wide Data

Long: each observation is a row (tidy)

<div class="subpoint">○ Observation does not necessarily mean "person" </div>

<div class="subpoint">○ Can be within-person measurements over time </div>

Wide: columns might represent different "values" of a variables


## Long vs. Wide Data

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r, echo=F}
dat <- data.frame(person = c("Harry", "Ron", "Hermione")) |>
  expand_grid(book = c("book 1", "book 2", "book 3")) |>
  mutate(score = rbinom(book, 3, .7))
dat
```
:::

::: {.column}
```{r, echo=F}
dat <- dat |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = person,
              names_from = book, values_from = score)
dat
```
:::
::::

Wide data common in spreadsheets, data from survey platforms

Long data typically easier to work with


## Key Functions

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
##### Wide to Long
`pivot_longer()`
```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: false
longdat <- dat |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c("book 1", "book 2", "book 3"),
               names_to = "book", values_to = "score")
longdat
```
:::

::: {.column}
##### Long to Wide
`pivot_wider()`
```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: false
widedat <- longdat |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = book, values_from = score)
widedat
```
:::
::::


## Key Functions

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
##### Wide to Long
`pivot_longer()`
<div class="subpoint-narrow">○ `cols` = set of columns to pivot </div>
<div class="subpoint-narrow">○ `names_to` = name of new column with the column names from before </div>
<div class="subpoint-narrow">○ `values_to` = name of new column with the values from before </div>
:::

::: {.column}
##### Long to Wide
`pivot_wider()`
<div class="subpoint-narrow">○ `names_from` = column with values to be column names </div>
<div class="subpoint-narrow">○ `values_from` = column with values to be in those columns </div>
:::
::::

## Transform

Usually, our data doesn't come to us with the variables exactly as we want them

Sometimes we need...

* New variables, based on our existing data or otherwise

* Summarized version of our dataset

* Reordered variables



## Transform: `tidyverse` syntax 

The `tidyverse` website mentioned that each package shares a common language for their functions

Based off of `dplyr` (one of the packages) verbs

::: blockquote
1. The first argument is always a dataframe.
2. The subsequent arguments typically describe which columns to operate on using the variable names (without quotes).
3. The output is always a new data frame.
:::

::: footer
<https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-transform.html#dplyr-basics>
:::


## More `tidyverse` syntax 

One more thing...

`tidyverse` verbs work best in a **pipe**: |>

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
How we've been using functions:

`output <- function(input)`
:::

::: {.column}
Functions in a pipe:

`output <- input |> function()`
:::
::::

Why is this helpful?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment}
Many functions together:

```
another_function(other_function(function(input)))
```
:::

::: {.column .fragment}
Functions in a pipe:

```
input |>
  function() |>
  other_function() |>
  another_function()
```
:::
::::

## Transform: Functions

A core few of the `tidyverse` functions...

::: {.panel-tabset style="font-size:90%"}
### `select()`

`select(df, columns)`

Selects just the columns you specify. Helpful for paring down data for easier viewing.

```{r}
player_minutes_played <- player_stats |>
  select(player_name, minutes_played) 

player_minutes_played |>
  head()
```

### `mutate()`

`mutate(df, new_column = ...)`

Adds new columns to the dataframe, either from scratch or based on existing columns. Can modify / overwrite existing columns as well.

```{r}
player_minutes_played |>
  mutate(hours_played = minutes_played / 60,
         hours_played_rounded = round(hours_played, 2)) |>
  head()
```

### `filter()`

::: panel-tabset
### Code Example

:::: {.columns style="font-size:80%"}
::: {.column width="50%"}
`filter(df, condition_to_keep)`

```{r}
player_minutes_played |>
  filter(minutes_played > quantile(minutes_played, probs = .99)) |>
  head()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
`filter_out(df, condition_to_toss)` does the opposite (as you'd expect by the name)

```{r}
player_minutes_played |>
  nrow()

player_minutes_played |>
  filter_out(minutes_played == 0) |>
  nrow()
```
:::
::::

### Logical Operators

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {style="font-size:80%"}

| Symbol | Meaning                   | 
|--------|---------------------------|
| `==`   | equal to                  |
| `!=`   | not equal to              |
| `<`    | less than                 |
| `<=`   | less than or equal to     |
| `>`    | greater than              |
| `>=`   | greater than or equal to  |

:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
1 == 1; "A" == "A"
9 + 10 > 5
"Georgia Tech" != "Georgia State"
c(1, 2, 3) >= c(3, 2, 1)
```
:::
::::

:::

### `summarize()`

`summarize(df, .by = optional_grouping_variable, new_column = ...)`

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
player_minutes_played |>
  summarize(mean = mean(minutes_played),
            median = median(minutes_played),
            min  = min(minutes_played),
            max = max(minutes_played))
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
player_stats |>
  summarize(.by = team_name,
            total_minutes_played = sum(minutes_played)) |>
  head()
```
:::

::::

### `arrange()`

`arrange(ordering_var)`

Orders data based on some variable. Can use `desc()` (descending) to flip.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
player_stats |>
  select(team_name, player_name, minutes_played) |>
  arrange(player_name) |>
  head()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
player_stats |>
  select(team_name, player_name, minutes_played) |>
  arrange(desc(minutes_played)) |>
  head()
```
:::
::::

:::


## Transform: Questions

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
1. What team had the most goals overall?

```{r}
total_goals_df <- player_stats |>
  summarize(.by = team_name,
            total_goals = sum(goals))

total_goals_df |>
  arrange(desc(total_goals)) |>
  head(10)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
total_goals_df |>
  filter(total_goals == max(total_goals))
```
:::
::::


## Transform: Questions

2. What goalie had the highest saves per match played?

```{r}
player_stats$position |> unique()

player_stats |>
  filter(when_all(position == "GK",
                  matches_played > 0)) |>
  select(team_name, player_name, saves, matches_played) |>
  mutate(saves_per_match = saves / matches_played) |>
  arrange(desc(saves_per_match)) |>
  head()
```

# Simulation


## Simulation

Simulating fake data is such a helpful skill to have in your toolbox. You can...

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="66%"}
- Check that methods are working correctly
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="33%"}
```{r}
rnorm(1000000, 5, 10) |> mean()
```
:::
::::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="66%"}
- Build your intuition and understanding about statistical theory
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="33%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-align: center
n_reps <- 100000
tibble(n = n_reps,
       sd = c(1, 1.25, 1.5)) |>
  uncount(n_reps) |>
  mutate(draw = rnorm(n(), 0, sd)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = draw, group = factor(sd))) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4, color = NA, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(
    data = tibble(sd = c(1, 1.25, 1.5), 
                  height = dnorm(0, 0, sd) * 0.875,
                  draw = 0),
    aes(label = paste("SD =", sd), y = height),
    color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 4.5
  ) +
  guides(y = guide_none(NULL),
         x = guide_axis(NULL, cap = T),
         color = guide_legend("SD")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-4, 4)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
n_reps <- 100000
tibble(n = n_reps,
```

## Simulation Example: CLT

The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) says that the sampling distribution of the mean of any distribution with finite mean and variance will converge to be normal with increasing sample size.

::: subpoint
○ Imagine: take a sample of $N$ observations from the population, calculate some statistics (e.g., the mean), and toss them back.
:::

::: subpoint
○ Repeat a whole bunch of times
:::

::: subpoint
○ Sampling distribution: the distribution of those calculated statistics (e.g., means)
:::

Let's say we're not so sure, and we want to test this out with different distributions and sample sizes $N$.


## Simulation Example: CLT

Before simulating, define your goals / questions.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Questions

Does the sampling distribution of the mean really converge to normal for wonky asymmetrical distributions like the $\chi^2$ distribution?

At what sample sizes does this fail?
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Goals

See if the distribution of means from repeatedly sampling data looks normal

::: subpoint-narrow
○ Does this change with different original distributions from which the data is drawn?
:::

::: subpoint-narrow
○ Does this change with sample size? 
:::

:::
::::


## Simulation Example: CLT

Then, sketch out a plan. Try to build things up step-by-step, not all at once.

1. Start with data sampled from a normal distribution. Generate one sample of data, take its mean.

2. Repeat this process multiple times, generating replications of data samples and sample means.

3. Visualize both: the original distribution of the data (sample distribution), the distribution of the the samples' means (sampling distribution).

4. Incorporate different distributions.

5. Incorporate different sample sizes.


## Simulation Example: CLT

1. Start with data sampled from a normal distribution. Generate one sample of data, take its mean.


:::: {.columns style="font-size:80%"}
::: {.column width="50%"}
`rnorm(x, mean, sd)` where `x` is the number of samples

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
samples <- rnorm(3, mean = 1, sd = 0.5)
samples
mean(samples)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Instead of having it in a vector by itself, lets put it in a dataframe

```{r}
sim_data <- tibble(x = rnorm(3, mean = 1, sd = 0.5))
sim_data
mean(sim_data$x)
```

:::
::::

::: {.callout-note style="font-size:80%"}
### `tibble()`
A `tibble()` is just like a dataframe, but better. The best part is its printing---`tibble()`s will never crowd your screen by trying to show every single value of a dataframe. Also, they work better with making `tibble`s in `tibble`s in `tibble`s... [More on `tibble`s here](https://tibble.tidyverse.org/articles/tibble.html).
:::


## Simulation Example: CLT

2. Repeat this process multiple times, generating replications of data samples and sample means.

:::: {.columns style="font-size:80%"}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Let's specify the sample size and how many replications we want. Start small!

```{r}
n_reps <- 2
sample_size <- 3
# total number of simulated draws
total_n <- n_reps * sample_size
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Let's create a `tibble` with a row for every index in every replication.
```{r}
sim_data <- tibble(
  n_reps = n_reps,
  sample_size = sample_size
) |>
  uncount(n_reps, .id = "rep") |>
  uncount(sample_size, .id = "index")
sim_data
```

:::
::::


## Simulation Example: CLT

2. Repeat this process multiple times, generating replications of data samples and sample means.

:::: {.columns style="font-size:80%"}
::: {.column width="50%"}
We can then draw `n_reps * sample_size = total_n` values from a normal distribution with `rnorm()`.

```{r}
sim_data <- tibble(
  n_reps = n_reps,
  sample_size = sample_size
) |>
  uncount(n_reps, .id = "rep") |>
  uncount(sample_size, .id = "index") |>
  mutate(
    draw = rnorm(total_n, mean = 1, sd = 0.5)
  )
sim_data
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
And, we can plot those draws (getting a head start on #3).

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
sim_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = draw)) +
  geom_density()
```

:::
::::


## Simulation Example: CLT

2. Repeat this process multiple times, generating replications of data samples and sample means.

3. Visualize both: the original distribution of the data (sample distribution), the distribution of the the samples' means (sampling distribution).

:::: {.columns style="font-size:80%"}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Let' finish out #2 by `summarize()`ing our `sim_data` into one sample mean per replication.

```{r}
means <- sim_data |>
  summarize(.by = rep,
            sample_mean = mean(draw))
means
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
And, we can plot those draws (getting a head start on #4).

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
means |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sample_mean)) +
  geom_density()
```
:::
::::


## Simulation Example: CLT

Before we start incorporating other conditions, let's scale this up.

:::: {.columns style="font-size:80%"}
::: {.column width="50%"}
We can then draw `n_reps * sample_size = total_n` values from a normal distribution with `rnorm()`.

```{r}
n_reps <- 1000
sample_size <- 10
total_n <- n_reps * sample_size

sim_data <- tibble(
  n_reps = n_reps,
  sample_size = sample_size
) |>
  uncount(n_reps, .id = "rep") |>
  uncount(sample_size, .id = "index") |>
  mutate(
    draw = rnorm(total_n, mean = 1, sd = 0.5)
  )
sim_data
```

## Simulation Example: CLT

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
4. Incorporate different distributions.

`runif(x, min, max)` where all values between `min` and `max` have an equal chance of being sampled

```{r}
uniform_samples <- runif(5, min = -1, max = 3)
uniform_samples
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
`rchisq(x, df)` where `df` is the degrees of freedom for the distribution

```{r}
chisquared_samples <- rchisq(5, df = 1)
chisquared_samples
```
:::
::::


## Simulation Example: CLT

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
4. Incorporate different distributions.

```{r}
n_reps <- 1000
sample_size <- 10
total_n <- n_reps * sample_size

sim_data <- tibble(
  n_reps = n_reps,
  sample_size = sample_size
) |>
  uncount(n_reps, .id = "rep") |>
  uncount(sample_size, .id = "index") |>
  mutate(
    draw_normal = rnorm(total_n, mean = 1, sd = 0.5),
    draw_uniform = runif(total_n, min = -1, max = 3),
    draw_chisquared = rchisq(total_n, df = 1)
  )
sim_data
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
We want to plot these draws as distributions, but `facet_wrap(~ grouping_var)` or `aes(fill / color)` are all expecting the values to be in one column, and a grouping variable that distinguishes them in another column.

```{r}
#| echo: false
tibble(grouping_var = rep(c("group_1", "group_2"), times = 3),
       y = runif(6, -3, 3) |> round(1))
```

:::
::::

4. Incorporate different distributions.

We can then draw `n_reps * sample_size = total_n` values from a normal distribution with `rnorm()`.

```{r}
n_reps <- 1000
sample_size <- 10
total_n <- n_reps * sample_size

sim_data <- tibble(
  n_reps = n_reps,
  sample_size = sample_size
) |>
  uncount(n_reps, .id = "rep") |>
  uncount(sample_size, .id = "index") |>
  mutate(
    draw_normal = rnorm(total_n, mean = 1, sd = 0.5),
    draw_uniform = runif(total_n, min = -1, max = 3),
    draw_chisquared = rchisq(total_n, df = 1)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("draw"),
               names_to = "distribution", values_to = "draw")
sim_data
```
:::

And grab their means.

```{r}
means <- sim_data |>
  summarize(.by = c(rep, distribution),
            sample_mean = mean(draw))
means
```

## Simulation Example: CLT

::::: {.columns style="font-size:80%"}
:::: {.column width="50%"}
5. Incorporate different sample sizes.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Our Sim

We can expand `sample_size` to be a vector of desired sample sizes

Because `n_reps` is length one, it will be "recycled" (repeated) to match the length of `sample_size`

For more complicated designs, we might have to use an `expand()` function

```{r}
n_reps <- 3
sample_size <- c(1, 3)
total_n <- n_reps * sample_size

tibble(
  n_reps = n_reps,
  sample_size = sample_size
)
```

### `expand_grid()`

Let's say we also wanted to vary `n_reps`

```{r}
n_reps <- c(100, 1000)
sample_size <- c(1, 3)

tibble(
  n_reps = n_reps,
  sample_size = sample_size
)

tibble(n_reps = n_reps) |>
  expand_grid(sample_size = sample_size)
```
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
n_reps <- 3
sample_size <- c(1, 3)

tibble(
  n_reps = n_reps,
  sample_size = sample_size
) |>
  uncount(n_reps, .id = "rep") |>
  uncount(sample_size, .id = "sample_id", .remove = F)
```
::::
:::::


## Simulation Example: CLT

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
5. Incorporate different sample sizes.

```{r}
n_reps <- 1000
sample_size <- c(3, 10, 30, 100)
total_n <- sum(n_reps * sample_size)

sim_data <- tibble(
  n_reps = n_reps,
  sample_size = sample_size
) |>
  uncount(n_reps, .id = "rep") |>
  uncount(sample_size, .id = "index", .remove = F) |>
  mutate(
    draw_normal = rnorm(total_n, mean = 1, sd = 0.5),
    draw_uniform = runif(total_n, min = -1, max = 3),
    draw_chisquared = rchisq(total_n, df = 1)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("draw"),
               names_to = "distribution", values_to = "draw")
sim_data
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
means <- sim_data |>
  summarize(.by = c(rep, distribution, sample_size),
            sample_mean = mean(draw))
means
```

## Simulation Example: CLT

5. Incorporate different sample sizes.

Now, let's think about how we want to visualize these results. We now have two condition variables (`sample_size` and `distribution`). We need to plot in a way that distinguishes both factors.

::::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="50%"}
### `facet_grid()`

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center
sim_data |>
  filter(rep %in% sample(n_reps, size = 30)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = draw, group = interaction(distribution, rep))) +
  geom_density() +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14) +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T),
         y = guide_axis(cap = T),
         color = guide_none()) +
  facet_grid(sample_size ~ distribution) +
  labs(title = "Sample Distribution")
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
sim_data |>
  filter(rep %in% sample(n_reps, size = 30)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = draw, group = interaction(distribution, rep))) +
  geom_density() +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14) +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T),
         y = guide_axis(cap = T),
         color = guide_none()) +
  facet_grid(sample_size ~ distribution) +
  labs(title = "Sample Distribution")
```
:::

::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
### `{ggridges}`

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
sim_data |>
  filter(rep %in% sample(n_reps, size = 30)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = draw, y = distribution,
             color = distribution, group = interaction(distribution, rep))) +
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.8, fill = NA) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14) +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T),
         y = guide_axis(cap = T),
         color = guide_none()) +
  facet_wrap(~ sample_size) +
  labs(title = "Sample Distribution")
```

```{r}
  ggplot(aes(x = draw, y = distribution,
             color = distribution, group = interaction(distribution, rep))) +

  theme_classic(base_size = 14) +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T),
         y = guide_axis(cap = T),
```
